summary: Describes the individuals and organizations involved in the IETF, including the IESG, the working groups, and the relationship with the Internet Society. It is a best current practice, and it was replaced by RFC 9281.

plainLanguage.summary:
This memo is a map of who does what in the IETF. It explains the difference between a working group, the people who run it, and the groups that approve the result.

It was written in 1996 and has since been replaced, so it describes the organisation as it stood at that time.

questions: who is involved in the ietf
what do the iesg and working groups do
what is the difference between the ietf and the iab
subtitle: A who's who of the people and bodies that produce Internet standards, as of 1996.

tldr.problem: An Internet standard is written by people nobody has heard of, in groups that have no formal membership list, under rules that few outsiders know. That makes it hard to see who decides what.
tldr.mechanism: The memo names the roles one by one: the RFC Editor, the Working Group chair, the Document Editor, the working groups themselves, and the bodies around them, the IAB, the IESG, IANA and the Internet Society.
tldr.outcome: It was a Best Current Practice, and it was later replaced by RFC 9281. The memo says nothing about security, because it is about process rather than about protocols.

today: RFC 2028 is a Best Current Practice from October 1996 and has been obsoleted by RFC 9281. It describes the IETF's organisations as they stood at the time, so names and roles may since have changed.

sections.title: What This Memo Covers
sections.content:
This document describes the individuals and organizations involved in the IETF, including descriptions of the IESG, the IETF Working Groups and the relationship between the IETF and the Internet Society. It is a Best Current Practice document that specifies an Internet Best Current Practice for the Internet Community, and it requests discussion and suggestions for improvements.

The memo does not describe how standards are made. The process used by the Internet community for the standardization of protocols and procedures is described in a separate document, RFC 2026, which defines the stages in the standardization process, the requirements for moving a document between stages and the types of documents used during the process, and which also addresses the intellectual property rights and copyright issues associated with the standards process.

What this memo does is name the pieces: which individual holds which job, which organization is responsible for what, and how people are chosen for the roles that make the decisions.
sections.plainLanguage: It answers a narrower question than you might expect: not how a standard is written, but who does the writing and who signs it off.

sections.title: Key Individuals
sections.content:
Three individual roles are described. The RFC publication series is managed by an RFC Editor, which may in practice be one or more individuals, responsible both for the mechanics of RFC publication and for upholding the traditionally high technical and editorial standards of the RFC series. The functions of the RFC Editor are performed by one or more individuals or organizations selected in accordance with the procedures defined by the RFC Editor charter.

Each IETF Working Group is headed by a chair, or by co-chairs, with the responsibility for directing the group's activities, presiding over the group's meetings, and ensuring that the commitments of the group with respect to its role in the Internet standards process are met. The Working Group chair is the formal point of contact between the Working Group and the IESG, via the Area Director of the area to which the Working Group is assigned.

The Document Editor is the person or people a Working Group designates for a particular document. The Document Editor is responsible for ensuring that the contents of the document accurately reflect the decisions that have been made by the working group. As a general practice the Working Group chair and Document Editor positions are filled by different individuals, to help ensure that the resulting documents accurately reflect the consensus of the Working Group and that all processes are followed.
sections.plainLanguage: The chair runs the group and speaks for it. The document editor writes down what the group decided. Keeping those two jobs apart is deliberate, so that the writing reflects the group's consensus.

sections.title: Working Groups and Areas
sections.content:
The Internet Engineering Task Force is an open international community of network designers, operators, vendors and researchers concerned with the evolution of the Internet architecture and the smooth operation of the Internet. It is the principal body engaged in the development of new Internet Standard specifications.

The technical work of the IETF is done in its Working Groups, which are organized by topics into several Areas, for example routing, network management and security, under the coordination of Area Directors. Working Groups typically have a narrow focus and a lifetime bounded by completion of a specific task.

Membership in the IETF and its Working Groups is defined to be established solely and entirely by individual participation in IETF and Working Group activities. Participation is by individual technical contributors rather than by formal representatives of organizations, and anyone with the time and interest to do so is entitled and urged to participate actively in one or more Working Groups and to attend IETF meetings, which are held three times a year. In most cases active participation is possible through electronic mail alone, and Internet video conferencing is also being used to allow for remote participation.

To ensure a fair and open process, participants must be able to disclose, and must disclose to the Working Group chairs, any relevant current or pending intellectual property rights that are reasonably and personally known to them if they participate in discussions about a specific technology. New Working Groups are established within the IETF by explicit charter.
sections.plainLanguage: There is no membership list and no employer pays your way in. You join by turning up, mostly by email, and you are expected to say if your company has a stake in what is being discussed.

sections.title: The Bodies Around the IETF
sections.content:
The Internet Society is an international organization concerned with the growth and evolution of the worldwide Internet and with the social, political and technical issues that arise from its use. It has individual and organizational members and is managed by a Board of Trustees elected by the worldwide individual membership. Internet standardization is an organized activity of the ISOC, and the Board of Trustees is responsible for ratifying the procedures and rules of the Internet standards process.

The Internet Engineering Steering Group is the part of the Internet Society responsible for the management of the IETF technical activities. It administers the standards process according to the rules and procedures of RFC 2026, and it is responsible for the actions associated with the progression of a technical specification along the standards track, including the initial approval of new Working Groups and the final approval of specifications as Internet Standards. The IESG is composed of the IETF Area Directors and the chair of the IETF, who also serves as the chair of the IESG. Its members are nominated by a nominations committee, the Nomcom, and approved by the IAB.

The Internet Architecture Board is chartered by the Internet Society Trustees to provide oversight of the architecture of the Internet and its protocols. The IAB appoints the IETF chair, approves the other IESG candidates put forward by the nominating committee, and reviews and approves the charters of new Working Groups proposed for the IETF. It provides oversight of the process used to create Internet Standards and serves as an appeal board for complaints of improper execution of the standards process. Its members are nominated by the Nomcom and approved by the ISOC board, with the IETF chair sitting as an ex-officio member.

The Internet Assigned Numbers Authority is responsible for assigning the numbers, keywords and other parameters that protocol specifications need to be unique, such as version numbers, protocol numbers, port numbers and MIB numbers. IANA publishes tables of all currently assigned values in RFCs entitled Assigned Numbers and functions as the top of the pyramid for DNS and Internet Address assignment.

The IETF Secretariat performs the administrative functions necessary to support the activities of the IETF, and consists of the IETF Executive Director and staff. The Executive Director is the formal point of contact for matters concerning any and all aspects of the Internet standards process, and is responsible for maintaining the formal public record of the process.

The Internet Research Task Force is not directly involved in the standards process. It investigates topics considered too uncertain, too advanced or insufficiently well understood to be the subject of standardization. When an IRTF activity generates a specification sufficiently stable to be considered for standardization, that specification is processed through the IETF using the rules in this document. The IRTF is overseen by the Internet Research Steering Group, which consists of the chairs of the IRTF Working Groups.
sections.plainLanguage: One group writes the standards, another approves them, a third keeps the process honest, and a fourth hands out the numbers that the standards refer to.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo is explicit that security is not addressed in it. The document describes who takes part in the Internet standards process and how the organizations are arranged, and it says nothing about the security of the protocols that result or of the process itself. The intellectual property rights and copyright issues that do accompany the standards process are handled in the separate document that describes the process, RFC 2026.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo says so in one line: security is not its subject. It is about who does what, not about what the standards protect.

items.title: RFC Editor
items.text: Manages the RFC publication series: the mechanics of publication and the technical and editorial standards of the series.

items.title: Working Group chair
items.text: Directs the group's activities, presides over its meetings, and is the contact point between the group and the IESG.

items.title: Document Editor
items.text: Ensures that the document accurately reflects the decisions the working group made. Usually a different person from the chair.
